name: Onakantheeswarar Temple, Kanchipuram
deity: Shiva as Onakantheeswarar, in three lingams — Oneswarar, Kantheswarar and Jalandhareswarar — with Kamakshi of Kanchipuram as the common consort
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Thondai Nadu, sung in the Tevaram by Sundarar (8th century)
summary: At Onakanthanthali in Kanchipuram, three lingams recall the asuras Onan, Kanthan and Jalandhara, and the hymn in which Sundarar asked the Lord for help and, tradition says, saw golden tamarind fruit fall.

sections.history: Onakanthanthali, in the Panjupettai quarter on the northern side of Kanchipuram, is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and a Paadal Petra Sthalam of Thondai Nadu. Its hymn is Sundarar's, gathered in the seventh book of the Tirumurai, which dates the shrine's place in the Tevaram tradition to the eighth century. The name joins the thali, or temple, to Onan and Kanthan, two asuras whom tradition remembers as devotees of the Lord here. Like the other Shiva temples of the city, it has no separate shrine for the goddess, for Kamakshi of Kanchipuram is held to be the consort of them all. The temple is administered by the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department of Tamil Nadu.
sections.architecture: The temple is a small walled shrine in the Dravidian manner, notable for having three sanctums of Shiva instead of one. Two lingams, Oneswarar and Kantheswarar, stand in separate sanctums named for the asuras who worshipped them, and a third, Jalandhareswarar, is linked with the asura Jalandhara. The cluster of sanctums, each with its own story, gives this modest compound its character among the many temples of Kanchipuram.
sections.legends: Tradition holds that Onan and Kanthan — described in one telling as commanders in the host of the asura king Banasura — found a lingam in the forest that once covered this place and became its ardent worshippers, and the Lord took their names. The best-loved story is Sundarar's. Come here in want, he sang to the Lord, who is said to have hidden himself in a tamarind tree as the hymn went on; Sundarar sang on, and golden tamarind fruit fell from the tree. Devotees still sing this pathigam, believing it brings prosperity.
sections.festivals: Pradosham and Maha Shivaratri are kept with special worship at the three lingams, along with Karthigai Deepam and the Arudra Darshan of Margazhi. Many devotees come to recite Sundarar's hymn on days of personal need; confirm festival dates locally.
sections.experience: Onakanthanthali is a quiet shrine off the Arakkonam road, a short way from the Sarva Theertham tank. Visitors go from sanctum to sanctum among the three lingams and many recite Sundarar's pathigam for the welfare of their household. It sits easily in a day among Kanchipuram's other Tevaram temples, including Ekambareswarar, Kailasanathar and Thirumetrali.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most neighbourhood temples of Kanchipuram. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer areas, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is in Panjupettai, Kanchipuram, reached from the Kanchipuram–Arakkonam road past the Sarva Theertham tank; it is a short auto ride from the Kanchipuram bus stand and railway station. Kanchipuram is linked by road to Chennai, Chengalpattu, Vellore and Arakkonam; Chennai International Airport, roughly 70 km away, is the nearest airport.
